response.answer:
A 1,000 Wh (1 kWh) portable power station can run a surprising number of things: laptops, TVs, Wi-Fi routers, fans, mini fridges, and even some kitchen appliances.

The important distinction is how much power an appliance uses (watts) versus how long you can run it (watt-hours).

For a typical 1,000 Wh station, expect about 800–900 Wh of usable AC energy, accounting for inverter losses.

One big catch: battery capacity ≠ output power

A power station has two important ratings:

1,000 Wh capacity: How much energy it stores.

1,000 W or 1,800 W AC output: How much power it can deliver at once.

For example, a 1,000 Wh station with a 1,000 W inverter generally cannot run a 1,500 W space heater, even though the battery theoretically holds enough energy to power it for about 34 minutes.

Refrigerators, pumps, and compressors can also require a brief startup surge much higher than their running wattage.

My practical takeaway: A 1,000 Wh power station is excellent for electronics, lighting, fans, and short-term refrigeration. It's much less useful for heating, air conditioning, or sustained cooking.

Are you considering one primarily for home power outages, camping, or running appliances? That makes a big difference in whether 1,000 Wh is enough.
markup:
A **1,000 Wh (1 kWh) portable power station** can run a surprising number of things: laptops, TVs, Wi-Fi routers, fans, mini fridges, and even some kitchen appliances.

The important distinction is **how much power an appliance uses (watts)** versus **how long you can run it (watt-hours)**.

For a typical 1,000 Wh station, expect about **800–900 Wh of usable AC energy**, accounting for inverter losses.

## What can you actually run?

Here are realistic estimates assuming 850 Wh of usable energy.

| Device | Typical power draw | Estimated runtime |
|---|---:|---:|
| Smartphone charging | 10–20 W | 40–80 charges* |
| Wi-Fi router | 10 W | 85 hours |
| LED light bulb | 10 W | 85 hours |
| Laptop | 50 W | 17 hours |
| Electric fan | 40 W | 21 hours |
| 55-inch LED TV | 100 W | 8.5 hours |
| Desktop PC + monitor | 200 W | 4.3 hours |
| Mini fridge | 40–70 W average | 12–21 hours |
| Full-size refrigerator | 60–120 W average | 7–14 hours |
| CPAP machine | 30–60 W | 14–28 hours |
| Electric blanket | 100 W | 8.5 hours |
| Coffee maker | 1,000 W | 50 minutes |
| Microwave | 1,200 W input | 42 minutes |
| Electric kettle | 1,500 W | 34 minutes |
| Space heater | 1,500 W | 34 minutes |
| Window AC | 500–900 W | 1–1.7 hours |

<caption>*Phone charging assumes roughly 10–20 Wh per charge, including losses. Fridge runtimes use average consumption, including compressor cycling. Actual results vary.</caption>

## What does 1,000 Wh look like in real life?

  <row align=start gap={3}>
    <AsyncImage query="home office laptop monitor wifi router desk" aspectRatio="5:4" maxWidth="144px" shop_eligible={true}/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Working from home**

      Laptop (50 W) + monitor (30 W) + router (10 W)

      <title size="lg" color="default">~9.4 hours</title>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">90 W combined</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align=start gap={3}>
    <AsyncImage query="cozy living room flat screen television floor fan lamp" aspectRatio="5:4" maxWidth="144px" shop_eligible={true}/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Entertainment during an outage**

      TV (100 W) + fan (40 W) + LED lamp (10 W)

      <title size="lg" color="default">~5.7 hours</title>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">150 W combined</text>
    </box>
  </row>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align=start gap={3}>
    <AsyncImage query="camping tent portable refrigerator led lantern camping table" aspectRatio="5:4" maxWidth="144px" shop_eligible={true}/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **Camping setup**

      Portable fridge (30 W average) + lights (10 W) + charging devices (10 W)

      <title size="lg" color="default">~17 hours</title>
      <text color="secondary" size="xs">50 W average combined</text>
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

Adjust the total wattage of the devices you want to power.

{@body const [capacity,setCapacity] = DIL.useState(1000)}
{@body const runtime = capacity*0.85/watts}
{@body const fmt = h => h>=24 ? `${(h/24).toFixed(1)} days` : `${h.toFixed(1)} hours`}
<box border radius="2xl" padding={4} gap={3}>
  <box gap={1}>
    <text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">Estimated continuous runtime</text>
    <title size="2xl" color="default" tabularNums>{fmt(runtime)}</title>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Assuming 85% usable capacity and constant power draw</text>
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Power consumption**
    <title size="lg" tabularNums>{watts} W</title>
  </row>
  <slider min={10} max={1500} step={10} value={watts} onChange={setWatts}/>
  <row justify="between">
    <text color="tertiary" size="2xs">10 W</text>
    <text color="tertiary" size="2xs">1,500 W</text>
  </row>
  <text weight="medium" size="sm">Battery capacity</text>
  <radio-group value={String(capacity)} onChange={v=>setCapacity(Number(v))} direction="row">
    <radio value="500">500 Wh</radio>
    <radio value="1000">1,000 Wh</radio>
    <radio value="2000">2,000 Wh</radio>
  </radio-group>
</box>

## One big catch: battery capacity ≠ output power

A power station has two important ratings:

- **1,000 Wh capacity:** How much energy it stores.
- **1,000 W or 1,800 W AC output:** How much power it can deliver at once.

For example, a 1,000 Wh station with a 1,000 W inverter generally **cannot run a 1,500 W space heater**, even though the battery theoretically holds enough energy to power it for about 34 minutes.

Refrigerators, pumps, and compressors can also require a brief startup surge much higher than their running wattage.

**My practical takeaway:** A 1,000 Wh power station is excellent for electronics, lighting, fans, and short-term refrigeration. It's much less useful for heating, air conditioning, or sustained cooking.

Are you considering one primarily for **home power outages, camping, or running appliances**? That makes a big difference in whether 1,000 Wh is enough.
